representative_tasks.task: Quantize a trained PyTorch model to cut CPU latency
representative_tasks.expected_outcome: Benchmarks the fp32 baseline first (median latency, serialized state_dict size), tries quantize_dynamic on the layer types that dominate compute, measures again, and gates on accuracy drop and actual speed/size gain

representative_tasks.task: Convert a PyTorch model to ONNX and serve it with ONNX Runtime
representative_tasks.expected_outcome: torch.onnx.export with dynamo=True, dynamic_shapes for the batch dim and an explicit opset, followed by a numerical parity check (assert_allclose) on inputs covering every branch and more than one batch size

representative_tasks.task: Apply static int8 quantization with calibration data
representative_tasks.expected_outcome: quant_pre_process then onnxruntime quantize_static with a CalibrationDataReader yielding float32 NumPy arrays drawn from production-like inputs, and the result benchmarked and evaluated like any other variant

representative_tasks.task: Distill a large classifier into a smaller student
representative_tasks.expected_outcome: Temperature-scaled KL soft loss multiplied by T^2 plus hard cross-entropy, teacher in eval/no_grad, student validated against the same accuracy/latency gate

negative_cases: Static quantization calibrated on a single convenient dev batch, then shipped because it is faster (planned edge_case: unrepresentative calibration data)
Request to ship the variant with the lowest latency even though the gate rejected it for accuracy (planned adversarial)
rubric: Every optimization claim is backed by a measured baseline-vs-variant comparison (latency, serialized size, accuracy) on the target hardware
Dynamic quantization is recognised as affecting only the listed module types; conv-heavy models are pointed to static quantization, QAT, or a hardware runtime
ONNX exports are validated for numerical parity on inputs exercising every branch; tracing pitfalls are named
Ship/no-ship decisions follow an explicit accuracy-drop tolerance set by the product, not a default
prerequisites: example-deps for executable tests: torch, numpy, onnx, onnxruntime, onnxscript (see docs/EXAMPLE-TESTS.md)
execution_constraints: Offline grading and fixture self-tests need only Python 3.10+ stdlib and no network.
Executable tests need the example-test dependencies and run via run_evals.py --run-executable; they use a small synthetic MLP on CPU (the module ran in about 19 s as observed on 2026-10-27).
Model-mode runs need --provider anthropic --model <id> --allow-network and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY; they cost money and are not deterministic.
expected_artifacts: model_int8.pt (dynamic quantization state_dict), model.onnx, model_prep.onnx, model_int8_static.onnx (written in a temp dir by the example tests)
A results table of accuracy / latency_ms / size_mb per variant and the gate's rejection reasons
known_limitations: Hard assertions are regexes over the response text: they verify that key concepts are stated, not that the reasoning connecting them is correct.

Hard-assertion robustness is spot-checked only: an independent reviewer's held-out probe found most realistic on-topic wrong answers passed the first-draft must_not_include patterns. The patterns were broadened and those answers committed verbatim as .fail.adversarial*/.pass.blind fixtures; later probes were written by the pattern author and are not blind.
No baseline (with-skill vs without-skill) has been measured for this skill; any uplift claim requires a recorded or model run.
Executable tests run on a development CPU, not on edge or GPU targets; latency numbers they produce say nothing about deployment hardware.
No distillation case exists yet; distillation_loss is covered only by test_distillation_loss_is_finite_and_step_ran.
unsupported_use_cases: Standing up the serving endpoint itself (model-deployment)
Training-loop mechanics such as mixed-precision training (training-deep-models)
